speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This conversation with Mahlon Follett took place at his home in Genesee on May 3rd, 1976. The interviewer is Sam Schrager.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, just personal things, you know, things that happened to me.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were a little kid? Like what?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I can remember one thing for instance I... Well, I don't know, I must have been about... I couldn't have been over three years old, maybe four, I don't know, just a little fellow. And I run away and I went over to the neighbors and they were, gosh, I believe a mile away. And the folks never missed me until I was gone a while. Of course they called in all the hired men and started searching for them. I remember going over to the people, they were all lived there. In fact, there's one of them old boys that lives out there now that's a grandson. And I remember this old lady. She couldn't hear anything and she had an ear phone, it wasn't an ear phone. A horn? Yeah, a great big horn. And I remember, as little as I was then, I can remember putting that in the ear and wanting me to talk into it to her. And they didn't know who I was or I guess they didn't know. In a way they didn't notify the folks. I was there quite a little while before they finally found me. Of course they didn't have telephones the whole day, so there was no way about it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember why you ran away?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh no. I was just a little, I suppose, just wandering around really more than running away. I see.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember what the house was like that you lived in in the country?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, more or less. It wasn't very modern. But I can remember it. Of course after we moved off I used to go back and we'd add red to the place. We used to go out there quite often. So up until the time it burned I was out there quite often.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was living out there pretty isolated?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: It sure was. I think possibly that's why I'd ever took up farming. I can remember that. Oh I suppose I was in high school. I worked out there for people that read the place. I remember I had an uncle that was dead in Seattle and he was visiting over here with his brothers. They came out there and he came out in the field where I was working and talking to me. He says, do you like this farming?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I says, no I don't.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: He says, I didn't either. I can't see how he could stand. He was telling me how he didn't like it. That's why he went into the dentistry. He says, when you get through school I'll send you to dental college. But I never worked at all and I never did want to go to dental college as far as that goes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were your father's reasoning on getting out of farming and into something else?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well I don't know. I think possibly it was so that I could go to school. Partly. I don't think my dad ever cared too much for farming. He farmed a long time. I don't think he was really a very good farmer probably. I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Had he come to this country because his brothers were here? Had they all come together or what?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: His father and mother and brothers came out the year before he did. He came from the east and came to Arizona and worked at the mines down there. And was on the coast for a while and then came up here. I remember he was telling me that he came to Lewiston, my boat. And he told me about hiking up to Lewiston, up to his folks, this place out here where they lived. And he said there was a fence between Lewiston and the farm. He just hiked over the hills there and trailed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: About when do you think? About what year?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I don't know. In the 1880s some place.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It would have had to have been before 1986 when they brought the train in here.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, I don't know just what year it was. I think it was in the early 1880s. I never really did have too much history of my parents or grandparents. I often wondered why I didn't. I guess when you're a kid you don't pay too much attention to those things. And afterwards you wish you had found out more.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I think maybe your parents' generation didn't talk so much about it either. I have a feeling they often didn't tell their kids very much.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, that's possibly true. I was thinking of the day when someone asked me about my grandmother and they asked me what her maiden name was. I didn't know. I just don't know. However, I remember that she had brothers come here to visit by camp. I was real small. I can't remember what their names were.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there a family on every hundred and sixty when your parents were living in the country there?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: New Orleans, Mazama, one hundred and sixty. But there was, of course, lots more than there is now. None of that had more than that. Almost had more than a hundred and sixty. I shouldn't say most of them, but an awful lot of them. But I don't know. We lived out there, of course. And for what I worked out there, there was no RFDs, no telephones. No electricity, of course. I'll never appeal to them. I remember my dad used to come to town riding a horseback, a goody-other, driving ahead. I think he tried to get it about once a week or every two weeks or something. One of the things I just remember is coming home after McKiddly had been shot and told about it. He was quite impressed with me. I was just a little taught. But that was several days after it happened. Now you know it almost instantly, if anything like that happens.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he pretty upset at that event?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I don't remember. I remember he was coming home and telling us about it. I'm bringing a paper. I remember we used to get the spokesman review at that time. It was a twice a week paper. Twice a week spokesman review.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that that country living was difficult for the women, the wives? Do you think that for your mother that that was a rough living?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I suppose it was. Yeah, it must have been. They didn't have any modern convenience, of course. I really suppose it was pretty rough.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You moved into town and you were only about six?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I was only six.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What are some of your early memories of Genesee and what the town was like when you were first young and living here?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I don't really know. It was quite a bit more business here than it is, of course, lots more than it is now. It was three or four general stores. I remember when there were three hardware stores, a couple of hotels. And I had a lot of my spoons off Wallabra. So it was quite a business town. There were three little barns, black-wood shops.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there a lot of people living in town at the time?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I don't know if there was any more living in town than there is now. In fact, I doubt there was as many, but there was a little more around in the countryside. There were many more people living. Now, up the valley, there were schools up there that had just whole bunches of kids. I forget how many there were when he was going to school. But I can go out now and see where they used to be. I remember they used to be in the tabloids living. The buildings are all torn down now. So there was just an awful lot more people living.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the town full of life? A lot of people on the streets walking up and down and going in the stores? It has kind of a desolate feeling downtown now.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, I suppose it was. I don't remember really. The kids didn't impress you very much, was it?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Bustling.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Of course, the business houses didn't mean much to me in those days. My uncle started that store in 1896, since I'd been born.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know if he and his brother just had all the capital themselves they needed to go in, or if they had borrowed money or what they did?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I don't know, but I imagine that at least one of the brothers had the capital, because he sold his farm. I imagine that he put the money into the store. But of course, it didn't take near the capital. I think nowadays a few thousand dollars would set you up for quite a business. After I went to work at the store, my father, the young father that was working in there myself, was cleaning out the basement one day. We ran across the pile of old invoices. I got one of them. That was Robert Johnson Rand Shoe Company. An invoice, oh, that long. I don't recall now why it came to, but it wasn't too much money. It must have been a whole carload of shoes that they bought at that time. It was quite interesting, because prices were pretty low. Anyway, everybody was looking at it there. My uncle kind of remembered it, of course. I remember the shoe salesman came in shortly after that. We showed him this invoice back in 1896. He wanted to know if he could have it, and we told him, yeah. So he sent it back to the company that happened to be the same year they started business. So he said, well, they had it framed, and the office is back there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder, now, when your uncle started that store in 1896, Rosenstein's store was here, wasn't it?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Levi's store was here.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I don't know about Levi's. I can't remember Levi's, if it's possible. I remember there was a Levi's here, but Rosenstein's, I remember, were here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But that didn't stop your uncles from thinking that they could have a business of their own.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, no. No, they was, well, it was Rosenstein's that was a store. One time there had been a Vollmer store, I think. I don't know who it was. I remember a man named Markson was running it over across the street where the Fast Time Pool Hall is now. There was one on the corner where the corner bar was, probably in the opposite, and it was running that. And so there was at least four general stores. All of them had a little of everything, except meat. At that time, none of the stores had meat. There was one and sometimes two or three meat markets. All was one, and every once in a while somebody would start up another one. Like restrooms, they'd start up and last a short time and pull over.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Seems like they were a lot more casual about going into business and going out of business when they were young.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yes. Lots of businesses started up and didn't last long. But these three or four general stores, they lasted for, well, even after I was in the store, there was three for a while, and then it went down to two of us. And that's how the store and me had one.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Had your uncles had experience in a store prior to their starting it here?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, no. No, they were just, they were pretty young fellows. They started up. No, I'm sure any one of them, one of them, as I said, had been a farmer, sold his farm.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they have help in the store? Did they have wives that worked in them too?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yeah. Fred Vollett's wife worked in there a bit at the time. Well, they used to hire several clerks. When I first came to work in there, there was six or seven working in the store. Three bar dudes. They had a lady hired. And Jackson's son and myself, so there was quite a few of us. But of course there was lots more business. No automobiles, or not many at least. Roadworks are good. And the country population was a bunch more. We used to stay up on Saturday nights, and that was the busy time. Everybody came to town on Saturday nights. All the hired men would come in, and of course they'd buy clothing and stuff. Lots of times it'd be eleven or twelve o'clock before we'd get closed up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Families would come in on Saturday nights. Would the whole family come?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Lots of times, yeah. It was pretty busy on a Saturday night. And they'd all come in to the barbershop too. There was all those 33 barbershops. And they'd all have baths. They'd come in and take baths in the barbershops.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Really, they had baths in the barbershops?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, they had all sorts of 33 bath tubs in there. Well, you take on a farm, you never get a bath until you came to town. That is, I mean, the family probably would. I mean, the hired men, they wouldn't have any place for them. I think now, most of them have showers. They don't take another thing. They can take a bath every day. That time you'd go a long time between baths. I don't think it was sanitary probably, but nobody thought anything about it. Because it just wasn't there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I would think it would be even kind of a hardship for the farm family too. With all the problems you'd have.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yeah, wouldn't they?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: To heat all that water.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: They'd have to heat boilers or somewhere, or other on the stoves.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, now had you ever worked in the store when you were growing up?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No. No, I never had. I didn't work there after the war. I backed up at the time when I had been working in Spokane for a couple years at the bank. I worked at the bank here for a while. I was going to business college and I came down and there was cashier. He'd lost his clerk in there, his teller, and I wanted to know if I wasn't going to work. I said, no, I wanted to finish school. He said, well, work for a while, then go back and finish school. I did. I worked for, I don't remember how long, six months or so. Then I went back and finished school. Then I went to work in Spokane Bank up until the time I missed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the business college you went to in Spokane? Yeah. Did you go there straight out of high school?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of, did you learn a lot at that college? Was it a good day?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, it was a pretty good school. It was an old Northwestern business college. It was in Higley, I believe it was, right? This Kinman was one of the professors in there. He was one of the teachers. He afterwards started Kinman Business College. I guess business college up there at the time, this Kinman Business College, of course, he isn't there anymore. He's not there anymore. He's gone. I guess he started, I know he started.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember how you happened to decide to go up there to go to college?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I don't. I don't really remember how. I had intended to go to university. I don't know. I went down to 1915 and went down to San Francisco to the fair. By the time I got back it was too late to enroll. I thought, well, go in the next year. In the meantime I was just going to business college. I never did go to university. The war came along. One thing, another.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you had the intention of going into business one way or another, in some form or another, probably?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I suppose so, yes. I remember when I did have a bot in.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why did you come to enlist in the Army?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, it was World War I. Everybody was either enlisted or drafted, most everybody of my age. I was in eighteen months, I think. I never got overseas until... ...send me to New York City for a year there. I was stationed in the city, the gas mask factory. Just a few of us. In the barracks, I think we had allowance for food and lodging. We lived where we pleased. Or for duty every day, just like you had a job.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I imagine living in New York City would be a little different than living in Genesee.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yes, it was. Of course, I'd lived in Spokane for a couple of years before I went there, so I really lived in a somewhat bigger place. Of course, not as big as New York. They... ...at that time they were awfully good, the fellows in uniform in New York City. We really had a good time there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean they...by good they were courteous or...?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, and it was...you could go down and print at any time and get free tickets to the shows... ...and half-price tickets and then uniform. And if you'd print at any time, if you'd register, you'd get it by a doctor there at some place. It was really good, sort of.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you writing in New York City?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Manhattan? Queens.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, I'm just to the other side of the Queensboro Bridge. Long Island side.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you enlist by yourself or were there friends of yours?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, there were several of us.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: From Genesee?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I was working at a backup Spokane. Oh. During three other sweaters at the same time. And we stayed together for a little while, but pretty quickly we was all separated.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that you boys at that time were enlisting because you felt patriotic... ...or was it because you figured you would be drafted anyway?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, probably a little of both, I would say.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I get some mixed feelings about that war when old timers talk to me about it. I mean, some people really didn't seem to have much use for it. And some of these people that were farm boys didn't really want to go. And they had to. And others seemed to think it was a good idea.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I think that was more true of the Second World War than the First. I think the First World War, they were pretty solidly behind the administration.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard it called the war to end all wars.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, that's what it's supposed to be. But there have been several since.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how come you wound up going into the store instead of sticking with the bank?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I don't know. My uncle wanted me because he wrote to me. He wanted to know if I would come in. Of course, I started in the bank just to get out of business college. I didn't have too good a job. I really intended to go back. When I came back, I went in there. They told me they had a job for me if I wanted to come back. But I thought probably this was a better opportunity going into the store. Because after all, those big banks should all get too far very soon. It's a slow process.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the store doing a big business?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, they were at that time. Yeah, they were doing a real good business at that time. They did for several years there and then they ran away. Of course, what hurt the small town was automobiles and good roads. Last year, two hours in the store, we didn't do much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When would you say that the business began to fall off?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I don't really know. It's all been going on for a long time. I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'm just real curious about trying to place it somewhat. Did it start to go down?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I suppose it started to go down. Then during the Depression in the 30s, it fell off. It was pretty bad there for a while. Then it boosted up a little better for a while. I think one reason it boosted up was there were fewer stores. Eventually, when we were the only general store, I think it was the Dunner Grocery Store and Dave Keel had a clothing store. We really were the only general store after it went to a halt.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Give me some idea of what people were buying from the store when you first were in there or even earlier. I'm curious to know what people were buying in the early days too.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: All kinds of clothing and groceries, of course. Groceries probably was the guide. There had been all kinds of clothing. Of course, the women used to do a lot of sewing. They used to sell a lot of peace goods. Women would buy jeeps and all that type of stuff. We sold an awful lot of shoes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This would be when you first were working in the store? When you say groceries, I had the idea that most farm families were trying to grow as much of their own edibles as they could. Is that true? Well, I've seen that. It was true.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: It was a little different type of groceries we sold in those early days than we sold in the later days. Most everything was in bulk, with packaged goods. Even coffee. We sold more coffee in bulk. We sold canned coffee. And of course, at that time, produce. There wasn't much of any produce that you'd get in outside of oranges and lemons. It's interesting, but...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So what would the kind of groceries be that most people were buying? Coffee, obviously, they couldn't grow. They'd buy that.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They'd buy salt and pepper and that kind of stuff.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I have a lot of crackling. Oh, that top stuff of cheese was the big seller. That wasn't packaged. We'd get it around and cut it up. And while the stuff was in bulk, they'd eat the glasses. I remember when I first went to work, they had a keg of glasses in the back room that they'd sell all over. But that was the last one they had. And one of the fellas left to spigot out a little bit and come down the next morning and it was a mess. That was the last of the glasses in bulk. I used to have vinegar. I used to sell a lot of kerosene. I remember on a Saturday night, I used to hate to see those five-gallon cans of kerosene come in. You'd have to fill them. I'd be off the car lot to get any on you or anything or get the other stuff. Everybody would come in with a case of eggs.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You would take those eggs and trade?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah. We'd ship a lot of eggs.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How much could you give them for eggs?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, gosh. I don't remember how much they got to me. I know they got off with cheap paraffron. A while back, he brought a bunch of time and offered him ten cents a dozen and he went and sold them for that. Took them down and gave them to another fella. But I don't remember that I ever bought any of them as low as that. Fifteen cents a dozen, I can't remember. But they buried them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you take other dairy products too or just eggs? Did you take milk and cream?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, no milk or cream. Eggs and butter. A lot of the farmers made butter too. That used to be somewhat of a headache because an awful lot of butter came in. Some of it wouldn't be too good. You couldn't get rid of it. That used to be kind of bad.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: There was a real variety in quality in the butter.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yes. Some of these, up the valley, there was quite a lot of Norwegian people. In fact, there still is quite a few out there. Of course, they're second and third generations. But these were people that... And they made real good, practically all of them made real good butter. There wasn't any problem to sell them there, but some of the others had brought butter in pretty bad.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would be the matter with it?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, they were strong. They didn't know how to make it, I guess. I don't know about butter baking. No, I don't. But I know some of them was pretty bad.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, gosh, what could you do in a case like that? Would you tell them?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: A lot of it was sold out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, but you'd still give them credit for it?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah. You couldn't hardly tell them that their butter was no good. They should lose a customer.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So would you resell a lot of that butter to other people? Oh, yeah.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, most everybody bought country butter.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: People in town, you mean?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, people in town.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you didn't ship the butter out like you did the eggs? No, no.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: But eggs? Used to ship out an awful lot of eggs. Remember one long while, there was a full of them coming down from the main district. Gallag Wallace up in there used to come down to the pickup and take all the eggs he could get. He'd come down once a week. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I have heard that the credit that the stores extended was a mighty important factor to some of these farmers, many of the people in being able to get what they needed to live on.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah, there's a little doubt about that. At that time, people would pay their bill up in the fall and start a new one and run to the next fall. And it took quite a lot of capital up right then. You'd have to borrow the money to carry them with the bank. Very poor system, but that's the way it was. Of course, some of them never did pay. Depression years came along there. There was a thousand dollars on books that never were collected. That was probably the biggest headache of a small town merchant, this credit business.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, was it most of the families, did most farm families have to go to credit, or was it the exception rather than the rule?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I think most of them did. Of course, later years it got so they weren't quite so many, but in fact the last few years you couldn't carry them for the long of time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So the merchant would lose, it seems like he'd be in the middle there. You wouldn't be getting any interest on what you were owed, would you? No. You wouldn't be paying interest on what you borrowed from the bank.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, of course, kind of offset that was at that time, most of the people you bought from, the suppliers, gave a pretty good discount for payment within 10 days to some as high as 90 days. And your discount account would pay off more than what you borrowed. In other words, your discounts would more than offset what you borrowed at the bank. He's not going to borrow the money to pay these bills, but it paid to do it. And of course in the fall, if somebody paid up the bills you could pick up your notes at the bank and start all over again.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you find it to be a real headache to have to do it that way?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yes, it was.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It sounds like it would kind of leave you hanging from year to year.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: It did. Yeah, it was.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how did you know who you could trust?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, sometimes you find out to your sorrow that you didn't always trust. But the big majority of them were pretty substantial farmers around. But there was also a few that...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have any way of recovering when somebody...

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, as a general thing, they were pretty hard to collect. Oh, of course. Sometimes you could collect. We used to give some of our accounts to collecting agencies, the attorneys, one thing or another. They'd collect some of them. But mostly if you couldn't collect them yourself, why? It was just for our charge of all. Last few years, this Birch Association in Moscow used to collect some bills for us, they were about as successful as anybody.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Can you remember ever confronting, having to confront people and ask them?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder how you'd go about doing that. I don't suppose you'd have much choice.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah, you'd have to write to them and ask them for it. And some of them you'd be able to sort if you asked them for it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you find you had much change in the customers from year to year, or would you carry the same people year after year after year?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: More or less so, yes. It wasn't too much. It wasn't too much change. That is the farm accounts. Well, even the town accounts as far as that goes, there wasn't too much to go. Not like this now. I don't know how anybody could write a credit business file. But I used to know everybody in town, where they lived, what they did. Even knew all the kids, little kids in town. Now I go down and tile in on half the people anymore.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I just think about it. It seems to me that it would put you in a very difficult position if you had people that are local in their residence and they're not paying their bills to you. It's something between you and them. I would think it would be their responsibility to do that. I know if it was me, I would feel real bad if I had to start saying, you're not holding up your end of the deal here.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, that collectee was one of the worst parts of the business. And I never was a good collector.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you find a difference between, was there a big difference say, people on one hand who wanted to pay and genuinely couldn't because they couldn't afford it, and people who had it and didn't want to pay it?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I think in most cases it was people who just didn't have it. They'd get in too deep and couldn't get out. Of course in some cases it was deliberately being a bill, but in most cases it was they weren't able to pay.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Deliberately what? Beating?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: They would deliberately buy it with the idea of never paying it. But they weren't too many of that type.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well what happened when the depression hit? Did you just have to extend credit on a loan or two?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: You know it was rather strange at that time when the depression hit. People seemed to kind of realize we're all the same boat and really paid up better than they did before that. We didn't have the trouble collecting during the depression we did before. Of course the bills would be big and they'd be more careful, but they seemed to be feeling that they knew everybody needed the money and they'd pay up. Really, while business was pretty terrible during the depression, the collection wasn't as bad as you might think. Oh, once in a while you'd run across somebody that couldn't pay their bill for a year and they'd come in and tell you about it. You knew they wanted to, but couldn't. Maybe you'd carry them on for another year or something. Most of them would always pay though. They'd come in and talk to you about it. Why, they was the kind that would pay you, but some of them wouldn't even talk to you about it. The first thing you'd do is ask them whether they were even coming in anymore.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Probably don't know whether you'd rather not see them or see them.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's right. They'd be taking their business someplace where they knew they weren't going to be asked for the bill.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: For a while anyway.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's right.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, business fell off terribly during the depression. I'm wondering, what did people cut out that they had been buying before?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I really don't know. I couldn't say just what. I suppose they'd buy more staples and leave out the luxury items. It all went on less. Of course, that time the bank closing too, the failure of banks had hurt everybody. The old Genesee Exchange Bank was the main bank here. When it closed, it really hurt everybody.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did it close right at the banking holiday or was it before then? It was during the depression.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, I kind of think it closed before the bank holiday, but I'm not sure about that. I don't really remember.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How much?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Of course, they were a correspondent bank with the Exchange National in Spokane. The Exchange National went under. Of course, they had a big deposit up there, this bank. That hurt them. Probably was the reason for their failure as much as anything else.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think they made a big effort to stay afloat?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, I doubt they did. Of course, they were all local directors.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know if they tried to raise money in a subscription kind of deal? That's what they managed to do in Troy. They went out and sold more stock.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I don't think they did that here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Reorganized is what they did. Some of the people that had stock lost quite a bit of it, but people got it.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: They did here. Were you from Troy?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah. Not born there, but that's where I lived for a number of years. What kind of losses did people sustain who had money invested in the bank? I assume they did lose some of their money.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they get any return at all for what they had in the bank?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, the depositors did, yes. When they liquidated, I don't remember what percentage they paid out. They cleared several dividends. I got part of the bank. Of course, the receiver collected all the notes as much as he could. But it took a long time. Mm-hmm. You got some rock over there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, yes. Yes.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: What's he doing or anything?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He's working in his garden a lot. I spend a lot of time doing that. I still see him. When I drive by in the evenings, he used to always work in the front office there, a little office in front of the house. He's still there, the lights on. I don't know, he still sells insurance there. I think he's still very busy with a lot of people and entrust their financial affairs to him.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, he was well liked.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And they still do. I mean, people still do, people that he's worked with for years.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I was on the draft board with him. So I knew him. But I know a lot of people here back in Troy, or did. I don't know if they spent any more, but that time we used to get a lot of Troy checks we got on the local bank.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was this after the bank closed here or before?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, no, afterwards. After. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the store caught in a bind when the bank went under? Did you have much in the way of loans from that?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, not in that way. Of course, we lost what we had or delayed getting back what we had in the deposit, which wasn't too much. But people just couldn't pay their bills. We sent out checks, of course, to pay them in our bills. They all went back. And it was kind of hard to get ahold of money to pay for. To pick up these checks that bounced, that was hard. Some of the companies were, we'd have to try to tell them the circumstances. Some of them were very good about it, and some of them earned their money right now. Wouldn't give me any additional time, but most of them would give me time enough to scour around and get refinanced.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did business start picking up again as the 30s went on?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yes, it did. It picked up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was Rosenstein's store running when you got into mallets? Yeah. Was the old man still running the store? Were the proprietors of these stores like you and Rosenstein's friends or rivals?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, we were friendly enough. I don't remember we were so friendly with Rosenstein's. They weren't enemies or anything, but they weren't the type that people were not too friendly with, I guess. Of course, they were Jewish, and the town where they were the only Jews. So they didn't mingle with the other people very much. Well, the girls got so they did. But later years, when Emmett was running the store up there, he was real friendly. He used to borrow back and forth. We was out of something, boy, we'd go borrow from them. By subversive, they'd get an order for something they didn't have, and they'd come down and get it from us. We were all friendly, and then later when Dave Keough was in there, we were all friendly. We almost went fishing together, turned the tides of the year, and one thing or another. So there wasn't any key rivalry between the businesses. I don't know. I think really the days before I was there with the store, it was a borrow rivalry.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why do you figure that?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I don't know. I guess it's...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What people said, maybe, or what you picked up on. It sounds to me like, I do have the idea from talking to old timers around the country, around here, that people were devoted to the store they traded at.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, that's true.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Whatever store it was, some of them traded it, too, more than one, but if it was one store they'd trade with, they got a...and this was in the early days. They got a good situation going, and they kept it.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, that's true. Yeah, that's true. They...most of our customers, for instance, were pretty solid. They did all the trading. A lot of them were people who hardly ever come in our place. They'd trade these someplace else, but they were almost either of us.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there a competition as far as the prices in the early days?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yes, there was. There was some that...I don't know. Yeah, I guess there was. I almost had a few customers that came in. Well, I can get it up the street for a dime less.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'd trade it for a nickel bar candy.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, probably exaggerated a little on that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I know.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But did they have it like specials? I mean, these days, that's the way they used to have specials. Yeah.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I mean, it's to have... Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: One of the things I've heard about the country's old-time stores was that the proprietors would get each item for the buyers instead of it being self-service. Is that correct?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah. Yeah, they were no self-service. Up the door just before I went out of the store. In fact, we never had self-service as long as I was in the store. But it was beginning to get to be the thing about the time I went out. Yeah, they'd give you your order, and you'd put it up for them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They'd have it written down and hand it to you on a sheet of paper?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, possibly. Verbal? Verbal, they'd give it to you. You'd write it down, then put it up. Yeah, I can remember the days of the old thrash machines, why they'd come in with a big list of stuff, hand it to you, and then go out to do something else. By the time they came back, they expected you to have it put up for them, all ready to go. And you would.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This would be the roustabout?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yep. Yep. There used to be a lot of those try-outs that used to come over. I don't suppose any of that. A bunch are left. Charlie Smith, Olsen, Gorsuch, Paynes. I guess some of the Paynes are still in Troy. I guess they'd probably be about the grandest of them, though. One that used to run it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder why they came in from over there instead of the fellows around here doing their own thrashing.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, of course, I'd say they weren't all from over there. There were several thrashing outfits here, but when it was ready, there wouldn't be enough. Of course, everybody would be anxious to get it thrashed before storms hit it, so they'd come over and have quite a little run.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Sure were a lot of people from over around Troy that came and worked in the harvests here.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Homesteaders would be on the homestead and they'd leave it to come down and make a little money to have something to buy stuff with for the winter.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah. When I was in high school, I used to work out of the directory machines. And I noticed all of the several were from Troy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that called Smoltz, the confectionary in Tadway? It used to go in there when you were in...

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah. When we were in high school, that was where we hung out all the kids and things. It wasn't much of anything to do with those days, but hang on some place. Smoltz was the place. A confectionary in Rest Street. They did quite a big business. Well, on the first of them, Smoltz, he was a cigar baker. He made cigars. He had just a little bit of a place that he gradually began to butt in, you know, candy. Eventually they went into the confectionary business, made ice cream.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say hang out, was it okay for kids to just sit around in there? Oh yeah. You didn't have to be buying something and eating something? Oh no.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Of course, if you had any money, you bought something. Usually we didn't have too much money. Maybe somebody would come in a little bit for... It was kind of a general hangout for kids. Oh, you wouldn't stay in there all the time, of course. I was going to meet anybody, that would be the place to meet.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the store? Would people sit around in the store?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Quite a lot, yeah. In the early days. They'd come in the town, the ladies would come in there, and we had some stools over there. They'd sit around there quite a bit. Mostly the ladies? Yeah, the ladies. I guess the men probably went to the boulevard to slug. One thing or another the women would... Women used to do most of the buying in there. Nice grocery buying. Stuff of that type and dry goods. They used to have quite a bit of Indian trade in them. That first one was the store. My uncle got so he could understand them. Quite a bit of Indian. He could talk with them pretty good. But I never got so I couldn't. Some of them wouldn't talk English. They'd just point to what they wanted to. Were they good customers for the most part? Yeah, they were pretty good, but they had a peculiar habit of... They'd buy one item, bring it over, pay for it. They'd buy another. They'd buy a dozen items, they'd buy them all separate and settle up for it one at a time. Really? Oh yeah. You never see them at that... those old Indians. They'd buy one item at a time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder what their thinking was about that. I don't know.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I never knew none of the old Indians, thought that way. Of course the younger ones got a rip. But I never caught any of them. If they picked up anything, they'd bring it over to me and pay for it. I never caught them stealing anything. I think they were most ... I don't think the present generation are quite as honest as the old people were. The last few years, I had a little trouble with them sometimes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would these people live near, fairly near, Genesee?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, trade here? Yeah. There were several of them lived out. Well, there's still a lot of reservation land out here, Indian land, but some of them used to live out here. But you don't see much of them anymore, do you?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you give them credit too? No, you wouldn't be able to. They're paying you for each item.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I never ever. Not those old Indians. They're paid for every item. They never ask for credit.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what kind of social activities went on in town in these years, back before the Depression?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, there wasn't much. I was thinking, I don't know what we did at the time. The reason I was thinking about it was thinking there was five or six of us kids that were pretty good friends up until two grades in high school. We'd go out and chase around together. There wasn't much of anything to do Saturday night. There'd be movies, but outside of that there wouldn't be much going on. We'd just fool around. They used to have revival meetings all the time. We'd go to them regularly. I was as good as a show.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would that be right in town? Oh, yeah. Would they put up a tent?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, there were a few cases where they'd put up tents. There was a Methodist church over here. Two or three times a year they'd have what they called revival services. So outside, preachers would come in and eat and preach. Most of them were pretty radical. We used to get a kick out of...there was something to do, I guess. We used to go. We were like some of the present ones that didn't behave themselves. We always behaved all right. We never got in trouble in church. We used to get quite a kick out of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when you say they were pretty radical, the kind of preaching style, was it hellfire and brimstone?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, hellfire and brimstone. We were sure going to hell if you played cards or danced or did anything for the news. But of course another thing in those early days, there used to be lots of dances. They'd dance pretty every week. In town? In the wintertime, they'd be out in the country schools. They'd be dancing out there. Go for it. About once a week during the winter, if you had some transportation, a team or somebody to have a team, I'd go out to some of these country schools to dance, parties. Lots of parties.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How would a party be different from a dance? Well, play games at parties?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: They were, of course, we'd go out to the coast with slaves. We'd go out to some of these people who lived out short distances in the country and buy a group out. We'd go out there, usually dance, have an oyster feed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: In town, where were the dances held?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, there used to be a building down here that was originally built for armory. They later called it an opera house. Then eventually the school built it, bought it for a gym. They played basketball in it for years. That's where the dances were held. There's the public dances. And KP Lodge used to have a few dances in the area of the Dation dances.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: KP Lodge? What's that?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Knights of Pythias.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Knights of Pythias, sure.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: They were pretty active here for a while, for a long while. And their dances used to bring out quite a crowd. Practically everybody got invitations to it, unless it was something they absolutely didn't want.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: These regular dances that you'd have on Saturdays, were they attended by mostly just the young people, or was it all ages?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: All ages. All ages. And of course the under-married people used to go to all of them. And of course the under-people. I know for years after we were married, we used to go to all the dances. I never did like to dance very well, but we used to go all the time. And they'd come over from Uniontown to some extent. We'd get down there. That's about as far as you wanted to go with the team.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were the Knights of Pythias, did they have members mostly from the men in town in Genesee, or was it all around the country, or did they belong to it?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Mostly from the town, or the farmers rather. They had quite a membership at one time. Of course there was another thing, several lodges. There was AP's, non-fellows, wooden, mason's. That was another thing. I can remember my dad was, when we lived down this farm out here, he'd ride in a horseback to go to lodge. Six or seven miles. Gosh, I wouldn't do it nowadays. I wouldn't even drive in, I don't think to go.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Maybe the fellowship was important to you.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's right. They'd get out, but there wasn't much for them to do. Visit your neighbors maybe.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well in town, do you think that the people that lived in town, or let's say the business community on Main Street, did they know each other very well, cooperate quite a bit?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yes. Oh yeah. Of course I think in those days there was lots more visiting back and forth among the people. Of course they didn't have radio, television, anything of the kind. That was about all there was to do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think it was pretty much the same, and this is something that I've been quite interested in trying to figure, do you think it was pretty much the same in the country as the town and the way of visiting and friendship?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah. Well I think so, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Not much difference between the two places?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, so my early memory since I was on the farm was going to visit somebody and go over and have dinner and naps.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you do the same thing in town? Oh yeah. Visit another family in town? That's right. I've heard a lot about that in the country, but not very much about it in towns.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, they did hear it in town. I can never backtrack. All of a sudden anyway, either my folks would have a company or they'd be going someplace for dinner.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it a very small circle of friends they had, or a pretty big size one?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I suppose it was a rather small circle, I would say.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: If you were going to try to guess, would you say maybe two or three families or five or six families?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah, I'd say more than that, five or six or more families. And of course they were, out this side of town, were mostly all Germans.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: To the west?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, to the west. And up the valley was practically all our widgets. Well, south it was a little of everything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I imagine the different groups stuck together pretty much.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's right, and the different churches did too. If you were Catholic you didn't have anything to do with the Protestants. If you were Protestant you didn't have anything to do with the Catholics. Here on Good Friday, this last Good Friday, the Lutherans and the Catholics and the community church went together. And the priest and the Lutheran preacher preached part of the sermon in the community church. Well, years ago I wouldn't have, well I had never heard of such a thing as going a Catholic priest going into a private Protestant church or vice versa. A Protestant minister on Thanksgiving Eve, they had a big service at the Catholic church and all three ministers spoke. That's the difference a few years would make. I hadn't heard of it for many years ago or more.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there, in those early days, were there things that the whole community, regardless of nationality, would get together on? Or was it not, was there really just like four or five different communities here?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yeah, the dancers for instance, they'd come from all segments. And they used to have celebrations, Fourth of July, four shows, when they got together and the whole community would take part.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Sounds like you're saying the town then was a way, it was when people came to town that they became one community instead of different ones.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yeah, I guess so.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's kind of what it sounds like, saying I don't mean to put words into your mouth.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, they all were some different groups really got along pretty good. There wasn't any friction or anything. But naturally the Norwegians kind of clicked together, so the Germans more or less. I can remember when I first went to the store, a lot of the Norwegian ladies would come in the store. Boy, I'd have an awful time understanding them. They talked pretty broken. I got so I could. Nice ladies, but they talked pretty broken.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I think one of them didn't have much opportunity to learn the language being at home and with each other all the time.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's true. And of course a lot of them came over from Sweden or Norway.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They were already grown.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's right.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what nationality was your family?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I don't know on the father's side. I never did know it. My dad, he didn't know. He'd been American as far as I knew back. But on the mother's side, they were French-Canadians. My grandmother lived with us two, three years. She could talk better French. She could English.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, among the business people in town, were most of them American?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah. Yeah, they all were. They all were. I don't remember any of them that were. Yeah, they all were. I don't remember any of them that were.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This horse show on the Fourth of July, that brought in people from all over to town? Were they especially big celebrations?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, they were. They were pretty good-sized celebrations. I'd run them for two, three days. Pretty good-sized carnivals used to come in for them. They really used to have a big crowd. In Uniontown, they had a stock show down there. They showed both horses and cattle. This horse show's here. It wasn't bad enough horses. In Uniontown, that's a stock show. They used to get an awful crowd. And of course, people from here and get out there and they'd appear. Those were the days before tractors. Everything was horses. They used to be pretty competitive who'd have the best horses. And of course, in those days, every time I had a baseball team, by every Sunday, some place or other, They weren't big leagues, but they played pretty good baseball sometimes. At least it was always interesting.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Some of these little towns, they seem to have fights as a regular part of the baseball game. They'd fight with the other town.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, yeah, sometimes they'd get to almost to the verge of fighting the other way. It was a keen competition, especially between Uniontown and Juliaetta. But all the towns used to have Kendrick, Juliaetta, Troy, Uniontown, Colton, Genesee. Moscow.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, in Moscow I've heard, and around Moscow I've heard people say that there was a real difference between the people that were farm people lived in the country and the people that were town people lived in town. When the country people came into town, they stood out as being from the country. Would you say that would be true of Genesee too?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I wouldn't say so here. Possibly in a few cases it would be, but not very often. I suppose some families come to town and be pretty country-fied maybe, but most of them, they were all just the same.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think it had much effect that, I've had the idea that the farming around here was more developed than, you know, it was more developed further along than it was in most of this county, you know, in places where they've had to clear their homesteads?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, I imagine that's true. Of course, there was a lot of door land there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I imagine that there was really more prosperity around here because of that.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, I imagine that's true. I think in the early days, it's kind of gone the other way now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Gone the other way?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, the town isn't as good as a business town anymore than it used to be. I think, for instance, Troy or Kendrick or some of them are much better business towns than Genesee.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder why it's hurt Genesee more than it has a place like Troy.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I think possibly it's because of being about halfway between Lewiston and Moscow. Long ago Lewiston and long ago Moscow. And, uh, do that trade even. I don't even have a barber here anymore. Used to be two tea shops. Don't have a doctor. There used to be two doctors here. Never since I could remember up until the last few years. The last 20 years, I guess.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I guess people's loyalty to the town stops when they feel it gets too expensive maybe. Because you'd think that maybe if the town was serious enough about keeping some businesses and they patronized them enough they could keep them.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, people like to go where there's a better selection than one thing or another. When I first went to the store we used to have a little razor wire and one thing or another. Well, after a few years you couldn't handle that because you couldn't carry them from a selection. And like a larger base camp, it's the changing of the times.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, you mentioned the revivals a while ago. In Moscow they caused a lot of hot debate and really some disturbance because the one or two of them in particular attacked Moscow. In Moscow at all, that really did it. The whole business of drinking and dancing was pretty controversial in Moscow.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I guess it was the most loony town. The churches used to be pretty much against it when I was a kid. Playing cards was terrible. Now the ministers themselves play cards and everything. I don't think anything about it, but in the early days why?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that the revivals stopped people from playing cards and drinking?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I don't think it ever did. I don't think it did a bit of good. Probably didn't do any harm either, but I just doubt whether they ever had much effect on people. Maybe some of the older people. I can remember, we had a minister here, he was here for years, from the middle of the night. I don't know, he was here, he came here as a young fellow. He was in his first preaching position. He got so with everybody in town, Protestant, Catholic or anybody, he was a friend of theirs. One thing or another. I think possibly that kind of started people a little bit. To be a little broader minded, because before then a lot of people, a lot of the church people, thought that playing ball on Sunday was a terrible sin. And this middle of the night, he was a pretty fair pitcher. He used to play ball on Sunday himself. He used to tell a story about him, and he kept his uniform under his pulpit so he could make it when he had none on top. A little bit exaggerated. When he first started, by some of the older people in church, he didn't like it too well. After he'd been here a while, I guess he won him over.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So he pitched for the Genesee team.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: The town team, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well that's interesting.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I can see in my time, I'm much broader minded than all the churches have got.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there a lot of drinking at the dances during Prohibition when you were a fellow?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I would say a lot. There was some, of course. There was some. But it wasn't too bad. It didn't get really rough, most of the dances. If I got too bad, somebody used to take care of me, you know, out of the way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that the moonshine that was around was mostly locally produced or brought in from outside?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: All, I would say most of it was brought in. I don't think it was one or two that was doing a little manufacturing. One or two were caught up. I don't think there were very many steles around here. I think it was mostly all brought in.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The thing about that that I kind of wondered about this country around here is whether it was pretty well accepted, you know, for people to drink if they wanted to during those Prohibition times or if it was frowned upon pretty heavily.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I wouldn't know. I think it was kind of accepted, over the last, by a lot of people. Of course, some people never would brew it, of course. Prohibition, prohibition.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The prohibition itself probably didn't make too much difference about how they felt about it one way or the other.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: You know, I've always thought that maybe people were drinking during the Prohibition, that is, heavy drinkers drinking more than they have since or before. I think more people now take a social drink or two, but I don't think there's many that drink really get drunk like they did during the Prohibition.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Because it was illegal?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Because it was illegal, I guess. And I think more people started on it then. I told them they can't have it, why? They seemed to want it that much more. Now, practically everybody will take a drink, I would say everybody. You might have very few in a group, but if there's cocktails or something, no one will drink. That don't mean that very many of them get drunk.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there much town politics in Tennessee in the early years?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I don't think so. It was all the same. I wouldn't say a lot. I wouldn't say there was a lot of interest in politics. Although any political speaker can get quite a crowd out because there wasn't much else to do but go listen to them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I noticed in looking at some of the old things about Genesee that GAR was very prominent.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah. A few of them, when I was young...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, there are a couple more things I was thinking of asking about. Do you ever hear much about J.P. Vollmer?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Not anymore.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I know, but I mean back in those early days.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was his reputation?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I was still in the bank here at one time. Well, I guess before my time. I think he had a regular wholesale store here. See, they used to trade all the stuff from here up on the prairie. There was no railroad. There was Lewis. It had to be all out of here. This was the first railroad. And he owned the bank. It was a lot of land that he... You hear a lot of stories about him. Of course, I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I'll tell you the stories that I hear about him are not very complimentary. Because people say he got a lot of land from getting people over a barrel. That's true. And they're owing him money.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I guess there's no doubt about that. That's the impression I always got of him. Of course, I never knew him before my time. He was active. I think he was still alive back in the river. But his family were in the way. I worked in the bank here a while. He owned the bank, I know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He still owned it at that time.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah. His son-in-law was really running it. The bank didn't do much business because people didn't like the ballers.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it the only bank in town?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, there was two at that time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The other one got more of the business.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of the son-in-law?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I never really knew him. Only talked to him on the phone.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He wasn't actually here.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I think he was here a time or two, but I don't remember him at all. I just talked to him on the phone. I know what nobody in the bank liked. They might know that. I don't know whether it was because they had him or he was the father of the son-in-law.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there anything in the bank policies at the time that you were working there that was different from the other banks?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh no.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So it was more of the bad taste they had from the past?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: That's true.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did that bank fold before the other one did?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, it never did. It never folded up?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, was it still running?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: It closed up during the holiday, but it opened right up afterwards.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So is that still running in town?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, of course they sold out for security. But it never did close. Only for the holiday. I was working there. They didn't have much business.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the moving of the town from Old Town to this one? I know that was before your time, but I'm curious about what you heard about what caused that move.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, it was when the railroad came in. They came in this far and were intending to go on to get us to the Old Town. And whoever owned the land between Depot and up there, I know who I think owned it, but I see when they made up this history of the country, they claimed the rose estate owned it, but I don't think he did. But anyway, whoever owned the land wanted the much part the railroad wouldn't pay when they stopped right here. But the Depot here had stopped and moved on out. I suppose it's half a mile out from Old Town. So in order to get the railroad, they had to move.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they move much of the town from there to here, or did they abandon most of it?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I really don't know. They moved some of it, I know. Rose Estate had a store out there, and he moved that in. I've been running for quite a few years here in town. Well, I built this other building, which went all the way down. Otherwise, I don't know how many buildings were moved. I can remember as a little kid coming in from the farm, we used to come in through Old Town. There was, oh, I suppose maybe half a dozen buildings there at that time. A few people lived out there, I think.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: People lived in the town, in the Old Town, in some of those old buildings?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah. Yeah, there was a few people still in there after. Well, I suppose they had their places, and lived out their days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But no more stores there?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, no. No, not in my time. I was never here. There wasn't any business out there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, who do you think owned the land at that time?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I thought Platts did, but I may be wrong. I thought Todd Platt owned it. You know Kenny, probably. He'd be his grandfather. I think he owned the land, but I may be wrong. Because this history that they've got out, they say that Rosenstein did. Well, it don't make sense, hardly, that Rosenstein would have done anything to keep him coming out there, so that he'd have to move his store.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's a good point.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: It don't necessarily make sense.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: No, it doesn't figure.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I've also, when I was a kid, I always heard that it was Todd Platt, that he wanted too much for the land right away, for the whole road to go out there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: As I recall, Vollmer was the one that said that Rosenstein held him up, and this was in the early 1903 history. But you know, they used to say that about Vollmer and Troy, that he tried to hold him up in Troy. And that was part of why they changed the name from Vollmer to Troy, because he was trying to hold him up for more money, and the townspeople were very angry about that. Yeah.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, I really couldn't say for sure who was the responsible ones for moving the town.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A real bustling town for a while. Do you remember people talking about it being a real center of, I guess, before the railroad hit Lewiston, and then, as you say, there was all that traffic coming from the camp in Troy, too?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, Grangeville, they'd have to haul all the freight up there from here. They came here on the railroad, of course, I gave them my boat to Lewiston, but otherwise it was all hauled over on them. Of course, that was before my time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I heard a lot of people came, wound up coming here because it was the end of the track, the end of the line. And a lot of people also were waiting for the reservation to open up, too, for a settlement.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I suppose, maybe, I don't really know why. Lots of people, you kind of wonder how they ever happened to come here, all right, but I suppose they had some reason.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there any people that were kind of characters around town when you were?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah, yeah, it was awesome. Yeah, there was. Almost a few. I guess every town has them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Can you tell me in particular? Because I've heard, like I read from the real early days, but the only guys that I've heard about were Mike Driscoll, too.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Right about him, I think he was kind of a character, sub-author character.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, who was the sheriff when you were in town? There was still a sheriff, wasn't there?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: You mean county sheriff?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: No, I mean Town Marshal, really.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, there's been several, Hickman.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Hickman, yeah.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, he wasn't a particular character of any kind. He was all right. He was. You were on the limber barn here for years, then when the automobiles come along, he used to haul people in cars. Hire them to take them to those Moscow places. And later became Town Marshal. But he was, he wasn't what you'd call a character at all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I think of a character to me as kind of a guy that's a comical, you know, a guy that is a prankster and funny.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, that's why I said, Mike Driscoll, I heard a lot of stories about him. He was just a big Irishman and had a lot of fun. Kids used to play all kinds of tricks on him, I guess. I don't remember any of that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Kids used to play tricks on him, huh?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah, ...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: There were a lot of people coming in here at harvest time, looking for work, too. Oh, yeah. Like harvest tramps, they go on.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, hobos. Yeah, they used to have what they called a juggle down here. There'd be quite a few in it. It took a lot of them, a lot of them, to do the farm work during the days of binders and ... I'd go down there and hire these fellas. Some of them were pretty good, some of them no good. All kinds of people.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But the townspeople didn't mind having a jungle right on the edge of town there.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, I don't think so, though.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Didn't bother them.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I don't think so. Of course, I was in school at that time, and I don't know that it bothered anybody. Yeah. I know I rusted the air purthash machine. Used to send men to pick up a man or two. I'd get out there and pick up a couple. Maybe the next day I'd bring them back or bring a couple others.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You really didn't know what you were getting at?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: No, no. And some of them would stay all through the season.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you enjoy working in a thrashing crew? Did you find that to be good work or not?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, of course I was pretty young. I liked it all right, I guess. I don't remember that I disliked it particularly, either way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Quite a big operation, the impression I had.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yeah, it was. It was kind of interesting to look back at it, the way I don't know what I was so impressed with at the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I should be getting going. I don't know whether there's things we haven't hit upon. I don't know about anything like that. It does seem to me that Genesee, the town, was awfully important to the country, to the people. The farms, you know, for the training.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Yes, I guess it was at one time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It does seem to have changed more than most of the towns in the county.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: I think so. It seems like it. I think it's gone downhill faster. I know much more so than, well, Troy or Kendrick.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When would you say that the turning point would be when it started to decline? We were talking about this at the beginning, and I'm just wondering. I know it's hard to say, but if you're here...

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: It's hard to tell if it was gradual, of course. One thing had happened, then another. I wouldn't know what to say.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It sounded as though it never really recovered after the Depression.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, I imagine that's true. I don't think it ever did. It gradually began to go downhill. One after the other.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did your business dwindle a lot?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah. I could recall Tyler's 23 restaurants in town. Maybe three or four now, they can't support one. You'll have restaurants down. Of course, some didn't stay very long. ... was the only one that kept going, but some would be here for a few months and then fold. Of course, the hotel was kind of a dining room.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you, yourself, very seriously consider getting out of the grocery business and doing something else as the years went on here?

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Oh, yeah. I thought about it. I actually sold out one time. I was out there for a year. We bought a bag.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I guess you must have missed it, then.

speaker: Mahlon Follett
words: Well, it did. Yeah. Yeah, I guess after all, you grow up in a place and get used to doing something that's kind of hard to change. Yeah.
